replace

/rih-PLAYSS/ · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Replace means to put something or someone new in the place of another, or to take the place of.

Every January, Dad reminds us to replace the batteries in the smoke detectors, whether they seem dead or not.

Example

When the starting goalkeeper limped off with a twisted ankle in the second half, the coach sent in a rookie to replace her.

The rookie took the injured player's place — one person stepping into the position another held. Replace covers both patterns: you can replace something (swap it out) or one thing can replace another (take its spot).

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

substitute: Substitute means to put one thing in another's place as a stand-in, usually for a limited time — a substitute teacher covers the class until the regular one returns. Replace is the all-purpose word, and it usually means the change is meant to last. A substitute fills the place for a while; a replacement takes it over.

exchange: Exchange means to give one thing and take another in return — two directions at once, as with gifts, currency, or jerseys after a match. Replace moves one way only: the new comes in, the old goes out, and nothing is handed back. Trading jackets is an exchange; fitting a new zipper is a replacement.

supersede: Supersede means to take the place of something now outdated, making it obsolete — the new policy supersedes last year's manual. It is said of the newcomer itself, usually rules, systems, and versions. Replace is neutral about why and works for anything: batteries, players, worn parts.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

keep: to continue to have or use

retain: to hold on to something as is

Where it sits · how forcefully the old is displaced — swap → replace → supplant

swap vs. replace: A swap is a casual, friendly exchange of one thing for another — much lighter than replace, which puts something new in the old one's place for good.

supplant vs. replace: To supplant is stronger than to replace — it suggests pushing the old one out and taking over its position entirely.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — re-

Prefix — re-: back, again (Latin)

Root — place

Root — place: a spot, a position (from Latin platea, 'open space,' via Old French)

Put it together

Put it together: re- + place literally means 'to put back into a place' — and in modern use, to put something new into the place the old one held.

Use the root in a new word: misplace

Use the root in a new word: misplace: Coach called our confidence misplaced, then watched us win the sectional final by twenty points.

Root Check

Word Choice

everyday / neutral

Replace is a workhorse verb with two patterns worth noticing: 'replace X (with Y)' means swap the old one out ('replace the filter'), while 'X replaces Y' means X takes Y's position ('streaming replaced video stores'). Both are neutral and common in speech and writing alike.
